summary.text: For a prime \(p\), the proof derives \(v_p(\mathrm{numer}(m))=\sum_{i\ge1}\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor^2\) by counting pairs divisible by \(p^i\), and \(v_p(\mathrm{denom}(m))=\sum_{i\ge1}\sum_{r\le \lfloor m/p^i\rfloor} r\lfloor\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor/r\rfloor\) from Legendre’s factorial formula; the termwise bound of the inner sum by the corresponding square also establishes exact divisibility. Since \(\lfloor(np+k)/p^i\rfloor=\lfloor np/p^i\rfloor\) for every \(i\ge1\) when \(k<p\), both valuations—and therefore their difference, the quotient valuation—are unchanged.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N(m)=\prod_{1\le j\le m}\prod_{1\le k\le m}\gcd(j,k)
\quad\text{and}\quad
D(m)=\prod_{1\le k\le m}\left(\left\lfloor\frac m k\right\rfloor !\right)^k.
\]
Thus the sequence in the question is
\[
a(m)=\frac{N(m)}{D(m)},
\]
where the quotient is taken in the natural numbers. We will first prove that this quotient is exact and obtain formulas for its prime valuations.

For a prime \(q\), write \(\nu_q(x)\) for the exponent of \(q\) in the prime factorization of a positive integer \(x\). We use the elementary fact that if \(x<q^b\), then
\[
\nu_q(x)=\sum_{1\le i<b}\mathbf 1_{q^i\mid x},
\tag{1}
\]
where \(\mathbf 1_P\) is \(1\) if \(P\) holds and \(0\) otherwise. Indeed, the powers of \(q\) dividing \(x\) are precisely \(q,q^2,\ldots,q^{\nu_q(x)}\), and the hypothesis \(x<q^b\) ensures that no power with exponent at least \(b\) can divide \(x\).

We will also repeatedly use that, for every positive integer \(d\), the number of multiples of \(d\) in \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\) is
\[
\left\lfloor\frac m d\right\rfloor.
\tag{2}
\]

### 1. Valuation of the numerator

Fix a prime \(q\) and an integer \(b\) such that \(m<q^b\). Every \(j,k\) occurring in the numerator is positive and at most \(m\), so
\(\gcd(j,k)\le m<q^b\). Applying (1) to each greatest common divisor gives
\[
\nu_q(\gcd(j,k))
 =\sum_{1\le i<b}\mathbf 1_{q^i\mid \gcd(j,k)}.
\]
Now
\[
q^i\mid \gcd(j,k)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
q^i\mid j\ \text{and}\ q^i\mid k.
\]
Because valuations add over products, we may sum over all ordered pairs \((j,k)\) and interchange the finite sums:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nu_q(N(m))
&=\sum_{j=1}^m\sum_{k=1}^m\nu_q(\gcd(j,k))\\
&=\sum_{1\le i<b}
  \left(\sum_{j=1}^m\mathbf 1_{q^i\mid j}\right)
  \left(\sum_{k=1}^m\mathbf 1_{q^i\mid k}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
By (2), each parenthesized sum is \(\lfloor m/q^i\rfloor\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\nu_q(N(m))=\sum_{1\le i<b}
\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2.}
\tag{3}
\]

### 2. Valuation of the denominator

Define, for every nonnegative integer \(M\),
\[
g(M)=\sum_{k=1}^{M} k\left\lfloor\frac{M}{k}\right\rfloor.
\tag{4}
\]
We claim that if \(b\ge1\) and \(m<q^b\), then
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\nu_q(D(m))=\sum_{1\le i<b}g\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor\right).}
\tag{5}
\]

To prove this, first add the valuations of the factors in \(D(m)\):
\[
\nu_q(D(m))
 =\sum_{k=1}^m k\,\nu_q\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac m k\right\rfloor!\right).
\tag{6}
\]
Legendre's formula says that for every nonnegative integer \(r\),
\[
\nu_q(r!)=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac r{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\tag{7}
\]
Here \(r=\lfloor m/k\rfloor\le m<q^b\), so every term with \(i\ge b\) vanishes. Thus (6) becomes
\[
\nu_q(D(m))
 =\sum_{k=1}^m\sum_{1\le i<b}
 k\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/k\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Integer quotients associate in the form
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/k\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{m}{kq^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor
 \frac{\lfloor m/q^i\rfloor}{k}
 \right\rfloor.
\tag{8}
\]
Interchanging the two finite sums therefore gives
\[
\nu_q(D(m))
 =\sum_{1\le i<b}\sum_{k=1}^m
 k\left\lfloor
 \frac{\lfloor m/q^i\rfloor}{k}
 \right\rfloor.
\]
For a fixed \(i\), the inner summand is zero when
\(k>\lfloor m/q^i\rfloor\). We can consequently shorten that inner sum to
\(1\le k\le\lfloor m/q^i\rfloor\), and it is then exactly the function \(g\) from (4). This proves (5).

### 3. Exactness of the quotient

For every \(M\ge0\),
\[
g(M)\le M^2.
\tag{9}
\]
Indeed, for each \(1\le k\le M\),
\[
k\left\lfloor\frac Mk\right\rfloor\le M.
\]
There are \(M\) such terms, so their sum is at most \(M\cdot M=M^2\). The assertion is also immediate for \(M=0\).

Now fix any prime \(q\), and choose \(b\ge1\) large enough that \(m<q^b\). Comparing (3) and (5) term by term, and applying (9) with
\(M=\lfloor m/q^i\rfloor\), yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nu_q(D(m))
&=\sum_{1\le i<b}g\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac m{q^i}\right\rfloor\right)\\
&\le \sum_{1\le i<b}\left\lfloor\frac m{q^i}\right\rfloor^2
 =\nu_q(N(m)).
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}
\]
Both \(N(m)\) and \(D(m)\) are positive: factorials are positive, and every greatest common divisor appearing in \(N(m)\) is positive; when an indexing set is empty, its product is \(1\). By unique prime factorization, inequalities (10) for every prime \(q\) imply
\[
D(m)\mid N(m).
\tag{11}
\]
Thus the defining quotient for \(a(m)\) is exact. In particular, for every prime \(q\),
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\nu_q(a(m))=\nu_q(N(m))-\nu_q(D(m)).}
\tag{12}
\]

### 4. Invariance of all relevant floors

Let \(n\) be a positive integer, let \(p\) be prime, and let \(k\) satisfy
\(0\le k<p\). For every \(i\ge1\), we claim
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p^i}\right\rfloor.}
\tag{13}
\]
For \(i=1\), division with remainder gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p}\right\rfloor=n
 =\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p}\right\rfloor,
\]
because \(0\le k<p\). For general \(i\ge1\), divide first by \(p\) and then by \(p^{i-1}\). Associativity of integer quotients gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p^i}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor
\frac{\lfloor(np+k)/p\rfloor}{p^{i-1}}
\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac n{p^{i-1}}\right\rfloor,
\]
and exactly the same calculation for \(np\) gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p^i}\right\rfloor
=\left\lfloor\frac n{p^{i-1}}\right\rfloor.
\]
This proves (13).

To apply the finite formulas (3) and (5) simultaneously to \(np+k\) and \(np\), set
\[
B=np+p.
\]
Since \(k<p\),
\[
np+k<B.
\tag{14}
\]
Also \(B>0\), and the elementary inequality \(B<2^B\), together with \(p\ge2\), gives
\[
B<2^B\le p^B.
\tag{15}
\]
It follows from (14) and (15) that
\[
np+k<p^B.
\tag{16}
\]
The same conclusion holds for \(np\), since \(np\le np+k\) (or directly \(np<B<p^B\)). Thus the same truncation index \(B\) is valid for both arguments.

Applying (3) with \(q=p\) and \(b=B\), we obtain
\[
\nu_p(N(np+k))
 =\sum_{1\le i<B}
 \left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p^i}\right\rfloor^2.
\]
By (13), each term equals the corresponding term with \(np\) in place of \(np+k\). Hence
\[
\nu_p(N(np+k))
 =\sum_{1\le i<B}
 \left\lfloor\frac{np}{p^i}\right\rfloor^2
 =\nu_p(N(np)).
\tag{17}
\]

Likewise, formula (5) gives
\[
\nu_p(D(np+k))
 =\sum_{1\le i<B}
 g\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{np+k}{p^i}\right\rfloor\right).
\]
Again using (13) term by term,
\[
\nu_p(D(np+k))
 =\sum_{1\le i<B}
 g\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac{np}{p^i}\right\rfloor\right)
 =\nu_p(D(np)).
\tag{18}
\]

Finally, apply the quotient-valuation identity (12) at \(m=np+k\), then use (17) and (18):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nu_p(a(np+k))
&=\nu_p(N(np+k))-\nu_p(D(np+k))\\
&=\nu_p(N(np))-\nu_p(D(np))\\
&=\nu_p(a(np)).
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, for every positive integer \(n\), every prime \(p\), and every \(k\) with \(0\le k<p\),
\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+k))=\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np)).
\]
Taking \(k=0,1,\ldots,p-1\) proves
\[
\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np))
=\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+1))
=\cdots
=\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+p-1)),
\]
as required.
